title: Mud and spit (John 9:1–12)
hookLine: who sinned, this man or his parents? neither; he makes clay and says go wash
last: THE TRUTH SHALL MAKE YOU FREE.

cards: When something terrible happens, people reach for a reason. A diagnosis, an accident, a child born with a disability, and the question comes, out loud or whispered: what did they do to deserve this? It's an old question.
Jesus and his friends pass a man who has been blind since birth, and the disciples, without even lowering their voices, turn him into a theology problem.
"Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?" The man can hear them.

teach.h: NEITHER THIS MAN, NOR HIS PARENTS.
teach.b: The disciples give Jesus two choices, and he refuses both. "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him." Neither.
The blindness isn't a punishment. Christians have wrestled with the second half of that verse. Does it mean God made him blind just to make a point?

teach.h: WHERE DOES THE FULL STOP GO?
teach.b: Some readers answer by moving the full stop: neither this man sinned nor his parents. Period. Then: so that the works of God may be shown, we must work while it is day.
Read that way, Jesus doesn't explain the blindness. He moves straight from blame to work.
Then he does something earthy: "he spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay."

teach.h: MUD AND SPIT, LIKE DUST IN EDEN.
teach.b: Not a word from a distance this time, like with the official's son. Touch. Some early Christian writers saw an echo of Genesis, where God forms the first human from the dust of the ground.
Then: "Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, Sent.)" The man has to walk there still blind, mud on his face, through the streets of Jerusalem.

"He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing." And the pool is real: workers repairing a pipe in Jerusalem uncovered stone steps of a large pool from Jesus's time, which archaeologists identify as Siloam.

how: Christians often read this chapter in Lent, and many churches connect the washing in Siloam with baptism, which early Christians sometimes called illumination.

o: a healing spring where angels stirred water
the river where John the Baptist baptized
a Jerusalem pool; the name means Sent

games.q: you're blind from birth. a stranger puts mud on your eyes and says: go, wash in the pool of Siloam. what do you do?
o: wipe it off and ask for a real cure.
walk to the pool, mud and all, and wash.
wait for him to wash it off for you.
games.why: "he went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing." he had to walk there blind, trusting.

practice: Think of someone who is suffering, a friend, a stranger in the news, maybe yourself, and notice any quiet explanation in you: they should have known, they brought it on themselves, I must deserve this.

Don't argue with it; just notice it and set it down, then ask the question Jesus moved to instead: what work could I do here? If you pray, hold that person before God without explanations; if you don't, just hold them with care.

wordCard.voice: Siloam. The pool where Jesus sent a man born blind to wash off the clay, which John says means Sent.

orig.note: Greek form of Hebrew Shiloach. John translates it himself: Sent.

carryVoice: Your line: neither sinned. The blame stops there, and the work begins. See you tomorrow.
